cands.name: Peter Coe Verbica

money.note: Individuals gave $78,889; PAC money $3,500; candidate's own money $505. Percentages describe itemized individual gifts, which the FEC has processed through about July 2026.

cands.bio: Certified financial planner and managing director at Silicon Private Wealth, with a law degree from Santa Clara University and a graduate degree from MIT. Former adjunct economics professor at San Jose State. Ran for Board of Equalization District 2 in 2022 and U.S. House District 19 in 2026. Has held no elected office.

endorsements.text: Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association PAC (listed on his campaign website and in his Ballotpedia survey).

Self-reported in his 2026 Ballotpedia survey: former U.S. Rep. Tom Campbell, Jessica Patterson (chair emeritus, California Republican Party), SVGOP, Santa Cruz Republicans, Santa Cruz County Republican Central Committee, and the California Congress of Republicans.

cands.gaps: We found no legislative or governing record for this candidate, so there are no deeds to report. We found no stated positions on data centers, farmland or large development projects, foreign or institutional ownership of homes and land, policing and public order, gun laws, or abortion. We found nothing on teacher pay or on a legislative stance for school choice beyond a one-line campaign mention. We found no documented controversies. The pages did not say exactly where he grew up, beyond the family ranch and his San Jose-area schools.

end-homestead-tax.evidence: Says he supported efforts to stop tax increases, including Prop 50 in Santa Clara County, and has spoken against Santa Cruz County's Measure C, a tax on home sales. He also says he has presented a Prop 13-style statewide initiative strategy to the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association and the CAGOP.

slow-growth-protect-land.evidence: Lists reforming CEQA to allow more housing among his three key campaign messages.

workers-first.evidence: Calls for immigration reform that helps agriculture and high-tech businesses, including a 'Bracero 2.0' guest-worker program with a clear, expeditious path to legal employment.

school-choice-teachers.evidence: His campaign site lists school choice and merit-based education among the causes he advocates for.

roots.summary: Ballotpedia lists his birthplace as San Jose, and in his own 2022 survey he calls himself a fifth-generation Californian who grew up on a family cattle ranch; his schooling was at Bellarmine and Santa Clara University, and he lives in Santa Cruz County.

land_positions.quote_or_summary: Lists 'reform CEQA to allow for more housing' as part of his affordability message in his Ballotpedia Candidate Connection survey.

cands.bio: U.S. Representative for California's 19th District (represented the 20th District from 2017). Former Alameda County and Monterey County deputy district attorney and Navy Reserve intelligence officer who served in Afghanistan and received the Bronze Star. Son of former Defense Secretary Leon Panetta.

endorsements.text: 2026 endorsements listed by Ballotpedia include the Democratic Party of California, California Federation of Labor Unions AFL-CIO, California Teachers Association, California Environmental Voters, Equality California and the National Union of Healthcare Workers.

cands.gaps: We could not find when Panetta's family moved to California or where he lived as a young child. We found no statements or actions from him on data centers, ending homestead property taxes, limits on investor or foreign purchases of homes and land, slowing growth or protecting land, police pay and pensions, gun laws, or school choice and teacher pay. His campaign site is general on these topics, and he did not complete Ballotpedia's 2026 candidate survey. For immigration enforcement, we found only two bill votes reported by Ballotpedia, with no sponsored bills or statements.

votes.what: Final FY2026 spending package funding most remaining federal agencies through September 30, 2026.

votes.bill: S. 1071 / FY2026 National Defense Authorization Act (final)
votes.what: Final FY2026 defense policy and funding-authorization bill (about $900 billion), carried in the House on the vehicle S. 1071.

votes.bill: H.R. 5371 (2025) Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act, 2026 (Nov. 12 final, ended the shutdown)
votes.what: Ended the 43-day federal shutdown: funds government through Jan. 30, 2026 and three full-year spending bills.

votes.bill: H.R. 5371 (2025) Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act, 2026 (Sept. 19 House passage)
votes.what: House-passed stopgap funding bill to keep government open through Nov. 21, 2025; stalled in the Senate and a shutdown began Oct. 1.

votes.bill: H.R. 1 (2025) One Big Beautiful Bill Act (final passage)
votes.what: The 2025 reconciliation law: extends the 2017 tax cuts, adds new tax breaks, cuts Medicaid and food-assistance spending, and raises defense and border spending and the debt limit.

votes.bill: H.R. 881 (2025) DHS Restrictions on Confucius Institutes and Chinese Entities of Concern Act
votes.what: Bars Homeland Security funds going to Confucius Institutes and entities tied to the Chinese government.
Requires documentary proof of U.S. citizenship to register to vote in federal elections.

votes.bill: H.R. 1968 (2025) Full-Year Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act, 2025
votes.what: Funds the federal government through September 30, 2025 at roughly prior-year levels (March 2025 stopgap).

votes.bill: H.R. 152 (2025) Federal Disaster Assistance Coordination Act
votes.what: Streamlines coordination among federal agencies delivering disaster aid (hurricane/flood recovery).
Requires federal detention of undocumented immigrants charged with theft, burglary or assault of a police officer, and lets states sue over immigration enforcement.
